title: Colour and chemical safety: processing times and skin protection
audience: Mobile hairdressers and barbers who mix and apply colour, bleach and other hair chemicals at a client's location
learningOutcomes: Name the main hazards of hair colour, peroxide and powdered bleach, using the WorkSafe Victoria list
Apply processing times and mixing ratios from the product label, not from memory or habit
Describe the hazardous substances duties that apply to a self-employed or employing hairdresser in Victoria
referencesAtStart: Official references for this lesson: WorkSafe Victoria, Managing hazardous substances and irritants in the hairdressing and beauty industry (reviewed 12 September 2025); WorkSafe Victoria, Safety data sheets (reviewed 30 July 2022); WorkSafe Victoria, Hazardous substances: safety basics (reviewed 30 July 2022); WorkSafe Victoria, Globally Harmonized System of classification and labelling of chemicals (reviewed 22 November 2022); WorkSafe Victoria, Health and safety responsibilities (reviewed 3 April 2025); Safe Work Australia, New workplace exposure limits (WEL) to apply from 1 December 2026 (no date shown).

instruction.heading: The hazards in hair colour and bleach
instruction.body: Hair colour and bleach are chemical products used close to the face, eyes and skin, often in an enclosed room. WorkSafe Victoria's hairdressing and beauty page (reviewed 12/09/2025) names several hazards. The page calls PPD and hydrogen peroxide toxic and notes that both turn up widely in dye products. A typical peroxide product holds 7 to 12 per cent hydrogen peroxide, and stronger mixes carry more hazard. Powdered bleach contains persulphate salts that can irritate the eyes and nose, and even a small quantity of bleach dust is enough to irritate. Aerosol colours are classed as hazardous, and the page rules out their use on eyelashes and eyebrows. Hair sprays are usually treated as non-hazardous, though they can irritate skin and eyes. The page does not label any control as mandatory or suggested, so check the safety data sheet for the control it specifies, and treat the page's advice as guidance that supports the duties below.

instruction.heading: Processing times and mixing: follow the label
instruction.body: Processing time is the period a product is left on the hair or scalp before it is rinsed. It is set by the manufacturer for each product and each mix. A stylist who works from habit may leave a product on for longer than the label allows, which increases exposure to the skin and scalp. The safe rule is to set the timer from the label, mix only the quantity needed for the client, and check the mixing ratio before the product is applied. Your business's approved procedure for mixing and timing is recorded as {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}, and the products you use are listed in {{business:materials.approved_products}}. Where a product's label conflicts with a habit, follow the label. Where the label does not give a time for a service, stop and check with the manufacturer before the service continues.

instruction.heading: Duties, exposure limits and the change on 1 December 2026
instruction.body: WorkSafe Victoria's safety data sheet page (reviewed 30/07/2022) requires an up-to-date SDS to be held for every product, with access open to workers, contractors and emergency responders. Its safety basics page (reviewed 30/07/2022) says employers need a register listing every hazardous substance on site, and that workplace risks to health and safety need evaluating. A self-employed person carries a duty to keep others from harm arising from their work, limited to what is reasonably practicable. From 1 December 2026, Safe Work Australia states that the WEL schedule takes over from the WES schedule.

procedure: Read the safety data sheet and the product label before the first use of each product, and file the safety data sheet in the vehicle or kit
Set the mixing ratio from the label, mix only the amount needed for the client, and label the mixed product with name, date and dilution
Wear gloves and eye protection suitable for the product, and keep the mixing area separate from food and drink
Start the timer when the product is applied, using the processing time on the label, and do not extend it without checking the label
Use powdered bleach in a way that limits dust, and keep the lid on the container between uses
Never use an aerosol colour on eyebrows or eyelashes
Record the product, the mix, the processing time and any reaction on the job record

workedExamples.situation: A mobile hairdresser uses a powdered bleach at a client's home. The bleach makes a fine cloud when the lid is lifted, and the client's child is in the room.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the hairdresser do before continuing?
workedExamples.reasoning: WorkSafe says powdered bleach containing persulphate salts can irritate the eyes and nose, and that even a small quantity of dust irritates. The hairdresser should stop, move the mixing away from the child, close the lid, and mix in a way that limits dust. The product should be used according to the label and the safety data sheet, which may set dust controls. The incident should be recorded, and the business should review whether a dust-free product suits the service.

workedExamples.situation: A barber applies colour to a client and has a second client waiting. The label says 35 minutes, but the barber rinses at 25 minutes to fit the next booking.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is shortening the time an acceptable decision?
workedExamples.reasoning: The label sets the processing time for the product, and changing it changes the result and the exposure. The rinse time should not be changed to fit the schedule. The correct action is to plan the booking so that the full processing time is allowed, and to record any time change as an incident for review. Scheduling is covered in “Booking, travel routing and cancellation policy”.

equipmentAndPpe: Gloves rated for the chemical in use, changed between clients or when damaged
Eye protection where the product label or safety data sheet requires it
Non-slip apron or cape to protect clothing
Mixing bowls and brushes, cleaned after each use
Timer set from the product label
Container lids and labelled decant containers
Current safety data sheets for each product in the kit

commonErrors.error: Using the processing time a stylist remembers, not the one on the current label.
commonErrors.prevention: Read the label each time a product is used, and keep the label photo in the client record.

commonErrors.error: Storing mixed colour in an unlabelled container.
commonErrors.prevention: Label every decanted product with its identifier, date and dilution, as the business procedure requires.

commonErrors.error: Assuming an exposure limit from an old list still applies after the change.
commonErrors.prevention: Check exposure references after 1 December 2026, when the WEL schedule is due to take over from the WES schedule; state adoption is to be checked.

commonErrors.error: Treating a suggested control on the WorkSafe page as a legal requirement.
commonErrors.prevention: Label each control as mandatory or suggested, using the source, before it appears in a procedure.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: WorkSafe Victoria names PPD, hydrogen peroxide (7 to 12 per cent), powdered persulphate bleach and aerosol colours as hazards in hair products. These hazards are confirmed.

Employers must obtain and keep accessible the current SDS for each product and maintain a register listing hazardous substances (both reviewed 30/07/2022). These duties are confirmed for employers in Victoria.
From 1 December 2026, the WEL schedule takes over from the WES schedule, according to Safe Work Australia.
Monitoring requirements for hairdressers were not found on the pages checked.
The safety training in this lesson is not a licence or a certificate and does not authorise the use of any restricted product. Product-specific training is set by the manufacturer and the business.

qualityStandard: Every product has a safety data sheet on hand and a label check recorded before first use
Processing time on the job record matches the label time for every service
Every decanted product is labelled with identifier, date and dilution
Any dust, spill or exposure is recorded with the action taken
documentationEvidence: Safety data sheet register for the kit, with the date each sheet was last checked
Job record showing the product, the mix, the processing time and any reaction
Incident record for any spill, exposure, or dust event
Training record for each person who mixes or applies chemicals
summary: Colour and bleach carry named hazards, and WorkSafe Victoria confirms them
The label sets the processing time, and the business does not change it to fit the schedule
Employers' hazardous substances duties are confirmed in Victoria; the national exposure list changes on 1 December 2026
Completing this lesson does not certify any person to handle restricted products

knowledgeChecks.question: Which hazard does WorkSafe Victoria name for powdered bleach that contains persulphate salts?
options: Cuts from the powder particles, which can slice the skin on the hands
Irritation of the eyes and nose, and irritation from a small quantity of dust
Carbon monoxide from the mixing process, which builds up in small rooms

knowledgeChecks.question: A stylist's label says 35 minutes processing time, but the next client is waiting. What is the correct action?
options: Rinse at 25 minutes, because the next client is booked and the product is ready
Leave the product on for 45 minutes to be safe and avoid the risk of under-processing
Keep to 35 minutes and reschedule the booking, recording any change as an incident

knowledgeChecks.question: According to Safe Work Australia, what happens from 1 December 2026 to the exposure list?
options: The WES schedule gives way to the WEL schedule
The list is removed, and no exposure references are needed
The list stays the same, and only the label format changes
